The short answer is confidence. When people are confident about the economy, they will spend money more freely rather than hoarding it and waiting for a crash to occur. Banks will be more likely to offer loans to people if they believe the borrower will have success. Individuals are also more likely to invest when confidence is high. When people are worried about the economy they want their assets to be liquid. When they are confident that they will get returns on their investments, they will sacrifice some of that liquidity.

Have you ever seen It's a Wonderful Life? This scene with the bank run really does a good job demonstrating how the system is built on trust. Savings and loans are the foundation of our (the US) economic system, and people are only going to give their money to the bank if they trust that it will be there. In order to ensure that the bank can answer the demands of people who come looking for their money, they have to be selective about who they loan your money out to (in addition to meeting the federal minimums for cash on hand). Basically, when there is trust in the system, you increase the velocity of money. A high velocity of money is good for everyone, even the government (because they collect taxes almost everytime a dollar changes hands).

To answer your question, it depends on how you're measuring economic growth. The standard way would be to look at nominal GDP growth and real GDP growth. The real growth being adjusted for inflation - so in reality the real growth is the more accurate measure.

The basic formula to calculate a country's GDP is to add all consumption, investment, government spending, and the net value of exports minus imports (also known as the trade surplus or deficit, or the current account.)

So how does one increase these values?

Consumption: increases in the population will cause more income generally and an increase in consumption. Government transfers to the poor, where the marginal propensity to consume is basically 1.0 (sometimes higher). One could reduce taxes, however, this can have an adverse effect as a government will typically spend all of their tax revenues, whereas most households will save some of their earned income (tax policy is fun!) Increasing wages will have an effect as well, etc. etc.

Investment: this is capital investments by businesses and firms. I've not spent enough time studying the effects on investment so I'd rather someone with more experience take over here.

Government spending: This is all things the government spends their money on, less transfer payments. This is your military spending, medical spending, infrastructure spending, etc. If you have any questions here, feel free to ask.

Net exports: If a country exports more than it imports it will increase its GDP, simply put. The issue though is if you export too much you risk other countries not being able to pay you back. Likewise if your country imports too much it risks not being able to pay back its creditors. It's a balancing act.

This is your basics, let me know if you have any questions.
